description_full: Autotrader Group plc operates an automotive platform in the United Kingdom. The company operates through Autotrader and Autorama segments. It provides vehicle advertisement on its websites for private sellers, as well as insurance and loan finance products to consumers; and display advertising on its websites for manufacturers and their advertising agencies. The company also sells new vehicles and accessories; and facilitates the lease of new vehicles. It offers its products to retailers, home traders, and logistics customers. The company was formerly known as Auto Trader Group plc and changed its name to Autotrader Group plc in January 2026. The company was founded in 1977 and is headquartered in Manchester, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: AUTO TRADER GROUP PLC is a mid-cap communication services business with a $5.5B market cap on $834M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +12% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +2.4pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 47% against a 7% cost of capital — a 40-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 75% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $395M in free cash flow — roughly 47 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.10× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 81× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 11.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 62% operating margin runs 53pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 169 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 44% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 13% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 29% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 45% and a beta of 0.35, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $990 a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash and 42% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades only 9% below its DCF fair value of $7.99, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 33%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $5.78 to $11.60 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: EV/EBITDA 15.1 vs 9.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 7.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 2.6% annual cash-flow growth, 8pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 47% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 40pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.15).
It runs a 75% gross margin and converts 47% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.10x.
ROE of 72% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($24.3M of cash against $281.8M of debt), with interest covered 81.0x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 14.4, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 62% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 11.5% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 2% of profits supports about 1.1% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and institutions hold 79%.
It returns 11.1% a year to shareholders (8.8% in buybacks and 2.1% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 10 consecutive years.
people: With about 1,239 employees, each generates about $673K of revenue, in line with the Communication Services median.
That works out to $318K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.6M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
